items: In October 2026 Michael Saylor of Strategy (once MicroStrategy) pitched a ladder of new money: Bitcoin as digital capital, STRC as digital credit paying 12%, the company's shares as digital equity, and one day a dollar token paying 8%.

STRC is a preferred share, not a loan or a deposit. It has no end date, no right to your $100 back and no vote, and the company sets its 12% each month. Bitcoin covers it about 4 to 6 times today, and new borrowing would lower that.

Of 28 claims checked, 11 hold, 11 are spin, 3 are wrong and 3 cannot be checked. The numbers about today hold. The labels are where it slips: "strongest credit in the world" for a junk-rated issuer, and a dollar token paying 8% that US law does not allow.

The flywheel runs both ways. In 2025 Strategy bought more Bitcoin than was mined. In the third quarter of 2026 it raised $5.41 billion, spent only $0.59 billion on Bitcoin and sold Bitcoin to help pay dividends.

Money moving between baskets? Read three meters. Dollars: trades only move them, bank loans against Bitcoin create new ones. Ownership and risk: these cross, Bitcoin into listed companies, its risk onto savers. Market value: it changes with no dollar crossing.
Before you believe any account paying 12%, ask who promises the $100, where the 12% comes from, and what happens if the asset halves. Nothing here is advice.

items.text: Money sits in two baskets: Set 1, the old anchors (gold, government bonds, bank credit), and Set 2, the new rails (stablecoins, tokens, crypto). Stablecoins are Set 1 wearing Set 2 clothes.
Under the US GENIUS Act a compliant stablecoin holds cash, deposits or short bills, and may not pay holders interest.
A bond is a ticket you can resell. Free of default is not free of price.
A bank loan creates a new deposit. Repaying it destroys one.
Trades between people only move money. Banks also create it when they buy from someone who is not a bank.
Game theory asks each player's best move, given what the others might do.

new.text: Accounting and law, briefly. Since 2025 Strategy carries Bitcoin at market value, so reported profit swings with the price: $19.53 billion of net income in the third quarter of 2026 came from unrealized Bitcoin gains, not cash. The preferred shares sit in its accounts as temporary equity. Delaware law lets a company pay dividends only out of surplus, which on today's numbers binds only if Bitcoin falls to about $17,700 to $23,500. The founder's class B shares carry ten votes each, about a third of all votes on the company's share counts (to be confirmed in the proxy).

items: A saver moves $10,000 from a money market fund into STRC. The fund sells $10,000 of bills. If a household or another fund buys them, dollars only move. If a bank buys them, it creates a new deposit to pay. The saver's dollars go to Strategy.

Strategy buys $10,000 of Bitcoin from a miner or an early holder. The dollars go to the seller, who parks them in a bank, a bill or a money fund. No dollar enters Bitcoin. Bitcoin enters a listed company.
Strategy pays the saver a daily dividend from its dollar reserve, which was raised by selling new shares. In effect new shareholders pay the preferred holders.
In a bear market Strategy sells Bitcoin to pay the dividend. A Bitcoin buyer's dollars go to the saver, and Bitcoin leaves the wrapper. This happened in the third quarter of 2026.

A different door: a bank lends $10,000 to someone who pledges Bitcoin. The bank creates a new $10,000 deposit, so the new basket helps create old-basket dollars. Repaying destroys it. Saylor calls this a tailwind. Its size today is unknown: no public total was found.

why: RT 3.13 fifth step (bank loan creates deposits), court ledger fix on step 1 (bank buyer of the bill creates deposits, rb-moneymake). Word audit 'mostly'

new.label: What really crosses the line
new.text: In steps 1 to 4 dollars change hands inside the dollar basket, adding a little only if a bank buys the bills in step 1. What moves is ownership and risk: a listed company holds the Bitcoin in boom years, outside buyers in bust years, and the saver's claim on bills becomes a share resting on Bitcoin. In step 5 the owner's picture is literally true: pledged Bitcoin brings new dollars into being. And market value moves with no dollar crossing. So money does move between baskets, as ownership, risk and value, and at the edges as new money.

new.label: The ledger in detail: both floors, and the smaller channels

blocks.text: Two floors. Upstairs are bank reserves and the Fed's reverse repo. Downstairs are the deposits the public holds. A money fund that pays out by drawing on the Fed's reverse repo pushes new reserves and deposits into being, but money funds and other non-banks used only about $0.2 billion of it on 28 October 2026, so today the pipe barely touches the upstairs floor. Downstairs, the final buyer decides: a bill sold to a household or another fund only moves deposits, a bill sold to a bank creates them, and when Strategy's reserve buys bills from a bank, deposits shrink again. Nobody publishes who the final buyers were, so the net effect is not known.

items.q: You pay $100 for STRC. Where are your dollars a week later?

items.q: A bank lends you $10,000 against your Bitcoin. Did money move between baskets, or was new money made?
items.a: New money was made. The loan creates a new $10,000 deposit, backed by new-basket collateral. It is the clearest case where the new basket helps create old-basket dollars. When you repay, that money disappears again.
